dict.string:
Configure Zscaler Client Connector on iPhone and iPad — which cloud the device registers with, how the user is identified, and whether traffic is blocked when the tunnel is down.
On iOS these values are not delivered as a standalone app configuration: they go in the VendorConfig dictionary of a VPN payload whose VPNSubType is com.zscaler.zscaler. Build the dictionary here, then paste it into that payload’s custom data.
The human-readable description of this payload. This description appears on the Detail screen.
The human-readable name for the profile payload. The name appears on the Detail screen and doesn’t need to be unique.

The reverse-DNS-style identifier for the payload. This identifier is usually the same as the TopLevel value, with an additional appended component. This string must be unique within the profile. During a profile replacement, the system updates payloads with the same ‘PayloadIdentifier’ and ‘PayloadUUID’ in the old and new profiles.
The payload type, which each payload domain’s reference page specifies.

The globally unique identifier for the payload. The actual content is unimportant, but must be globally unique. In macOS, use ‘uuidgen’ to generate UUIDs. During a profile replacement, the system updates payloads with the same ‘PayloadIdentifier’ and ‘PayloadUUID’ in the old and new profiles.
The version of this specific payload.
The human-readable string containing the name of the organization that provides the profile. This value doesn’t need to match the organization payload value in the enclosing dictionary.

Name of the Zscaler cloud your organisation is provisioned on, without the top-level domain.
Enter ‘zscalertwo’ for zscalertwo.net, ‘zscloud’ for zscloud.net, and so on.
The iOS key is spelled all-lowercase — ‘cloudname’. Android and macOS use ‘cloudName’. The keys are case-sensitive, and a mis-cased key is silently ignored.

Domain your organisation authenticates with — the part after the @ in a user’s sign-in name.
Zscaler builds the login name by joining the Username below to this domain.

The part of the user’s sign-in name before the @.
Use your MDM’s partial-UPN variable so it is filled in per device — $USERNAME in Jamf Pro, {{partialupn}} in Intune.
If you set User Domain and Cloud Name, Zscaler expects Username and Device Token to be present too; leaving them out can stop the domain from taking effect.
Device token from the Zscaler Client Connector Portal, used to enrol shared or user-less devices without an interactive sign-in.
This value is a credential. Deliver it in an encrypted profile, never in a plain-text profile committed to source control, and rotate it if it is ever exported in the clear.

Whether traffic is blocked until Client Connector is connected and enforcing policy.
Enter 1 to enforce, 0 to allow traffic while disconnected.

Strict enforcement also needs a Policy Token, and an Exclude List for anything that must stay reachable while the tunnel is down — your identity provider first of all. Enable it without those and a device that cannot reach Zscaler cannot reach its login page either.
Policy token from the Zscaler Client Connector Portal. Required when Strict Enforcement is on.

Hosts that stay reachable while strict enforcement is blocking everything else.
List them comma-separated, with no spaces. Your identity provider and its CDN belong here.

Whether Client Connector uses FIPS-compliant cryptographic libraries.
Enter 1 to enable, 0 to disable.
